question:
What word does Chaucer NOT make a rhyme with in Book of the Duchess?

Answer Choices:
A. Wente
B. Here
C. Fool
D. Hool
E. Countour
F. None of the above

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: After reviewing the rhyme patterns in Book of the Duchess, I believe the answer is B. Here. Chaucer frequently pairs terms like "wente" with movement-related words, "fool" in contexts of folly or loss, "hool" with wholeness motifs, and "countour" in numerical or accounting imagery, but "here" does not appear to participate in any of the poem's sustained rhyme schemes around grief and dreaming, making it the clear exception among the options.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is E. Countour. Looking at the poem's structure, Chaucer repeatedly uses rhyme pairs involving words like "hool," "fool," and "wente" to build the dream-vision narrative, and "here" fits into several end-rhyme positions as well. "Countour," however, seems to appear more as a narrative term without being forced into a matching rhyme scheme in the same way—the meter and vowel sounds don't align as cleanly with the surrounding couplets, suggesting it's the outlier that Chaucer avoids rhyming. This feels consistent with how he handles technical or abstract nouns elsewhere in his early works.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

In the octosyllabic couplets of the *Book of the Duchess* Chaucer is constantly
closing a couplet on –ente, –ere, –ool words. 

* wente e.g. “I wente / I hente” etc. is a normal –ente couplet-closer in the
dream-vision;
* here / were, fere, etc. is a normal –ere couplet-closer;
* fool is a normal –ool closer and in the poem it is brought into a –ool
pair with its Middle English variant hool / whole, “I am a fool / hool” etc.;
* hool = whole, hale is the Middle English form that Chaucer regularly uses
in rhyme in the book and it is the partner of fool/cool in the –ool
rhymes.

*countour* ‘counter, counting-house’ is not a rhyme-position word in the
*Duchess*. The lexeme is essentially absent from the poem’s line-endings,
and hence Chaucer never makes a rhyme on *countour* in *Book of the Duchess*,
whereas the other four items are all attested as couplet rhymes in the work.
That is the only genuine non-rhyme of the set; in the usual loose sense
the poem does in fact rhyme on all four of Wente / Here / Fool / Hool.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: D. Hool

In the Book of the Duchess the rhyming couplets are consistently
Middle-English -ent, -ere, -ool, -our etc.  

* wente is regularly coupled with hente / shente, etc.
* here is regularly coupled with dere / fere / nere, etc.
* fool is regularly coupled with cool / tool / etc.
* countour / countoor is used in the couplet tradition and is
rhymed with tour / doul / sour etc.

The form hool is not a rhyme-partner that Chaucer actually employs in
the poem. The Middle English form that is used for ‘whole, hale’ is
hol / hole, and it is that form which is rhymed in the text. The
spelling hool never occurs as an active rhyme in the Book of the Duchess,
whereas the other four lexical items do occur as rhyme words.

In the octosyllabic couplets of the *Book of the Duchess* Chaucer is constantly rhyming his end-words in the normal way. 

*Wente* is a normal past of *winnen / go* and is used as a rhyme-word, e.g. wente / shente etc.; *here* is one of the most ordinary rhyme-words of the poem and is rhymed with *dere, fere, nere* etc.; *fool* is rhymed in the poem and the rhyme-pair that is normally quoted is *fool / hool*, *fool* ~ *cool* etc. *hool* = *whole, hol* is the ordinary Middle English form that is used as the rhyme partner of *fool*.

*countour* ‘counter, reckoner, accountant’ is not an item of the *Duchess* vocabulary and never occurs as a rhymed end-word in the poem. The word is found much later in Chaucer’s canon, e.g. in the *Canterbury Tales*, but not in the *Book of the Duchess*, so it is the only one of the list with which Chaucer does not make a rhyme in that work.

The Book of the Duchess is written in rhymed couplets and Chaucer uses a very
large stock of Middle English rhyme-words in it. Wente, here, fool/hool and
the whole/fool family all occur in the normal rhyming couplets of the poem,
e.g. wente ~ sente, here ~ dere/there, fool ~ cool and hool < ME hol ‘whole’
~ fool. The item countour ~ ‘counter, reckoner’ is not used as a rhyming
word in the Duchess. It is essentially unattested as a rhyme in the poem,
whereas the four other items are all met with in the usual Chaucerian
pairings.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: D. Hool

In the Duchess Chaucer is able to get a rhyme out of all of the forms that are
normally quoted from the poem.  `wente` is used in the regular -ente couplets
of the dream narrative, e.g.  wente / sente, `here` is the normal unstressed
deictic rhyme here / dere / fere, `fool` is the familiar fool / cool / wool
pairing of the lover’s self-mockery and `countour` occurs in the
descriptive passage on the lady’s estate and is rhymed in the -our class of
the poem.  The form that is quoted as hool is not the form Chaucer uses. 
The rhyme that is normally cited for the fool/wool couplet is wool,
*wolle*, and the Middle English form *hool* = ‘whole, hale’ is not set up
as a rhyme partner in the Book of the Duchess; the rhyme in the poem is the
fool / wool / cool family, not fool / hool.  Hence hool is the item in the
list that Chaucer does not make a rhyme with in the Duchess.

The octosyllabic couplets of the *Book of the Duchess* do rhyme on four of the items in the set and the fifth is essentially absent as a rhyme-end.

* Wente. The regular past of *gon* is a routine -ente closer in the dream narration, e.g. wente ~ sente / shente.
* Here. The deictic adverb is one of the most ordinary -ere closers in the poem, e.g. here ~ dere / there / fere / nere.
* Fool. The dreamer’s self-mockery and the Black Knight’s lament use the normal -ool class, e.g. fool ~ cool / pool / wool.
* Hool. The lemma ‘whole, hale’ is the regular rhyme partner of fool in the -ool class. In the Duchess the form is printed as hol / hole / whole / wolle, the normal Middle English spelling of the whole-lemma. That is the rhyme that is normally quoted as fool / hool / whole. Lexically the whole-lemma is rhymed with fool, so the item is present in the poem even if the exact modernisation hool is a normalisation of hol/hole.

Countour ‘counter, reckoner, counsellor’ is not used as a rhyme-ending in the *Duchess*. The lexeme is essentially absent from the poem’s line-endings; the -our rhyme class that is familiar from later Chaucer, countour ~ tournour / honour etc., is not exploited in this early dream-vision. The other four items are all attested as couplet rhymes in the work, with hool being orthographic variation for the attested hol/whole rhyme partner of fool. That makes Countour the genuine non-rhyme of the list.

The E cluster has the stronger textual case here. 2. Does countour occur/rhyme in Duchess at all?
